New Mexico State University Women’s Basketball

Session RPE Report – 2026-2027 Season

Dr. Luis Rodriguez Castellano

Data is current as of October 17, 2026

Report Overview

This report describes the New Mexico State University Women’s Basketball team’s training load, characterized by session rating of perceived exertion (sRPE), starting from June 01, 2026 through the current date. Sessions with main_focus = "OFF", athletes marked as DNP (Did-Not-Practice), and rows with zero duration/effort are excluded from descriptive statistics.

Coach A’s session ratings are presented alongside the team so that any divergence between how the coach perceived a session and how the athletes perceived the same session can be observed.

Coverage

  • Athletes tracked (excluding coach): 15
  • Distinct sessions: 124
  • Date range: Jun 16, 2026 – Oct 16, 2026
  • Team athlete-session entries: 897
  • Coach A entries: 94

4. Weekly Load Trends

4.1 Weekly Average sRPE, RPE Legs, and RPE Lungs

Weekly team-average of sRPE (bars) with two overlaid RPE lines: RPE Legs (black) and RPE Lungs (red). This separation reveals which type of effort is driving the perceived load week to week – muscular (legs) or cardiorespiratory (lungs). Divergence between the two lines highlights sessions whose demands were skewed toward one energy system.

4.1a Jump Height and Rebound DRI Trend

Team-averaged CMRJ Takeoff Jump Height (crimson, left axis) and Rebound DRI (black, right axis) across the same timeline as the sRPE/RPE chart above. Thin lines connect the actual team mean on each test date; thick translucent curves show the underlying trend after smoothing out noise. Watch for divergence between training load (above) and jump output: sustained high-sRPE weeks followed by downward trends here are an early fatigue signal.

4.2 Weekly Monotony and Strain

Monotony = mean weekly sRPE ÷ SD of daily sRPE within the week. High monotony (bars) means every day of that week looked the same in terms of load; that’s a risk factor when combined with high overall load. Strain = mean weekly sRPE × monotony. Peaks in strain (line) flag weeks where high overall load coincided with low day-to-day variability.

::: report-note Note on the week of July 27: monotony and strain appear exceptionally high because the week ended early (Fall break began mid-week) and the remaining sessions were highly similar in effort, including several zero-effort entries from Wednesday through Sunday. Low within-week variability inflates monotony, which in turn inflates strain, even though absolute load was not extreme. :::

4.3 Daily sRPE with EWMA Acute and Chronic Load

Daily team-average sRPE (bars) overlaid with the exponentially-weighted moving averages of acute (7-day) and chronic (28-day) load. When the acute line climbs above the chronic line, workload is accelerating; when it dips below, the athlete is de-loading or recovering.

4.4 Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR)

ACWR is the ratio of acute (recent) to chronic (baseline) training load. 0.8 to 1.3 is generally considered a safe “sweet spot”; >1.5 is the danger zone where injury risk climbs.Nontheless, this does not mean that danger is inminent, but more so that due to acute fatigue, the risk is higher.Pushing into this zone throughout a week is fine but once here, one must consider adjusting loads if performance begins to decline and other markers are showing negative trends. Moreover, underloading <0.8 can lead to under-training which can also lead to increased injury risk due to unpreparedness. Colored bands indicate these thresholds.

Interpretation caveat: after extended periods with little or no logged activity – such as early summer (week of June 22) or the return from Fall break (week of August 17) – the ACWR can appear unstable because the exponentially-weighted chronic load has not had enough recent data to normalize. Values immediately following a prolonged break should be read with that reset in mind.

5. Team vs Coach A Comparison

Side-by-side comparison of how the team perceived each session focus versus how Coach A rated it. Substantial gaps – particularly on the intensity metrics – signal that athlete internal response is diverging from coach prescription.

Interpretation caveat: discrepancies between how a coach rates a session and how athletes rate it may reflect lingering accumulated fatigue on the athlete’s side, which can shift their perception of subsequent sessions upward even when the coach’s prescribed intensity remains unchanged.

6. AM to PM Session Analysis

On days with both a morning (AM) and an afternoon (PM) session, does the morning effort predict the afternoon effort? Three views are provided so you can pick which best captures the effect.

Days with both AM and PM sessions across all athletes: 157

6.1 Scatter – Morning vs Afternoon RPE

6.2 Paired Difference (PM minus AM)

How to read the Paired Difference histograms: each bar counts how many AM-PM session pairs produced a given afternoon-minus-morning RPE difference. Bars at zero mean the athlete rated the two sessions identically; positive bars (right of the dashed line) mean the afternoon felt harder; negative bars (left of the dashed line) mean the morning felt harder. A distribution centered on zero with a tight spread suggests consistent effort between sessions; a distribution shifted away from zero suggests one time of day is systematically more demanding, and a wide spread indicates substantial athlete-to-athlete or day-to-day variability in how the two sessions were perceived.

6.3b Prior-Day to Next-Day RPE Correlation

Does yesterday’s effort predict today’s? For each (athlete, date) pair, this table lags the prior day’s RPE Legs, RPE Lungs, and sRPE values against the current day’s values. A strong positive correlation suggests high effort tends to persist from one day to the next – either because the athlete is accumulating fatigue, or because consecutive days of similar programming produce similar perceptions. Weak or near-zero correlations suggest each session is perceived on its own merits, independent of yesterday. Only athlete-dates with sessions on consecutive calendar days are included.

6.3c Load vs Performance Correlation Matrix

Pairwise correlations across the athlete-level load and performance indicators. All six values come straight from the database; weekly aggregation only groups existing values and does not derive new quantities. The subtitle shows how many athlete-week pairs supported the matrix.

6.3d Load vs Performance Correlation Matrix – Team-Week View

Same correlation idea as 6.3b, but each row is a team-week instead of an athlete-week. All athletes’ values are averaged into one weekly team mean before correlation. This matches the Section 4.1 chart’s granularity – one dot per week – but reduces statistical power (fewer observations). Useful if you want to see how the team’s collective weekly rhythm relates to collective jump output. Compare against 6.3b (athlete-week) to decide which lens to keep.

Reading the Load vs Performance matrices (6.3c and 6.3d): jump height appears largely unaffected by lower RPE Legs or RPE Lungs in isolation, although it tends to be depressed when the ACWR (based on EWMA acute-to-chronic ratio) is elevated. The Rebound DRI, in contrast, shows an inverse association with each individual RPE as well as with higher ACWR, suggesting that reactive-strength qualities may be more sensitive to accumulated and recent load than concentric-only output.

Data Notes

  • Source: daily_load table in aggie.sqlite, joined to athletes for role identification.
  • Season start: 2026-06-01 (parameterizable via YAML params).
  • Exclusions: main_focus = OFF rest days, DNP variants (“DNP-OUT”, “DNP-Coach Decision”, “DNP-OUT-Coach Decision”, “Kicked out of practice”), and zero-effort/zero-duration rows.
  • Anonymization: params$anonymize toggles between real names and anonymous_id. Coach A is identified by anonymous_id == "Player_AE" in both modes.
  • Anonymized render: rmarkdown::render(..., params = list(anonymize = TRUE))
